    A recent interaction with a translation agency reminded me of an important lesson: Legitimacy and professionalism are not the same thing.
    The company appeared legitimate. I received a real project, worked in a CAT tool. However, what concerned me was something else.

    After finding multiple negative reviews online, I decided to ask a few questions 📲.

    ➡️Me: "Would you be so kind to send me your LinkedIn profile?"
    ⬅️PM: "We have an official common LinkedIn. We do not have separate work LinkedIn IDs."
    ➡️Me: "Actually, the reviews on Trustpilot ✅ are really worrying. As I offer professional services, I need to be sure I establish reliable connections."
    ⬅️PM: "Don't worry about it, our firm is a legit company."
    ➡️Me: "Could you please send me some data that could verify your company registration and authenticity?"
    ⬅️PM: "I'll share your concern with our resources manager. I'm sure she'll be able to send you verified data."
    ⬅️PM: "Sometimes there are delays in payments because our end clients delay them. Other than that, there's never any discrepancy from our side."

    What struck me wasn't the content of the answers, but the pattern.
    Whenever I expressed concerns, I received reassurance.
    Whenever I asked for verification, I was told not to worry.
    But trust doesn't work that way.

    As freelancers, we're expected to prove who we are. We provide CVs, complete onboarding forms, sign NDAs, pass assessments, share references, and demonstrate our qualifications before being trusted with a project.
    Why should agencies be held to a lower standard?

    When a freelancer asks reasonable questions about company registration, payment practices, reputation, or the identity of the people they're dealing with, the answer shouldn't be "trust us." It should be transparency.

    To be clear, I'm not claiming the company was completely fraudulent.
    What I am saying is that professionalism is more than a website, a LinkedIn page, or a registered business. It's transparency, accountability, and the ability to withstand reasonable scrutiny. And if a company becomes uncomfortable when a freelancer performs due diligence, that alone is worth paying attention to.

    Have you ever declined cooperation with a client or agency not because you knew they were dishonest, but because the overall experience simply didn't feel professional?

    Fellow translators — quick warning ⚠️
    I was recently contacted about an “urgent” EN↔PL technical project (20k words, Trados, tight deadline — you know the drill). It looked fairly standard at first glance.

    Then came the catch:
    👉 register via a vendor portal link before seeing any files.
    Shortly after, a follow-up email said the project was “postponed” — but encouraged registration anyway.

    Curiosity kicked in, so I checked the link.
    Instead of a normal login or captcha, I got a “verification” screen instructing me to:
    • press Windows + R
    • paste (Ctrl + V)
    • press Enter
    This is NOT verification.

    This is a known malware delivery trick:
    The site silently copies a hidden PowerShell command to your clipboard. If you follow the steps, you execute it yourself — typically downloading a payload (often a credential stealer) in the background.
    No warnings. No prompts. Just compromise.

    ⚠️ Important:
    Nothing happens unless you paste and run it — but the social engineering is getting more convincing.

    I’m seeing more and more of these on ProZ lately:
    – generic “urgent” offers
    – no real project details
    – pressure to register via external links
    – poor personalization

    Please stay sharp:
    • never run commands from a website
    • don’t trust “verification” steps outside standard captchas
    • verify agencies independently
    • trust your gut when something feels off

    The volume of scams is increasing — and they’re getting smarter.
    Stay safe out there. 🕵️‍♂️
